minds.title: The Existentialist
minds.concern: The role of consciousness and project in defining meaning.

debate.speaker: The Relationship Critic
debate.text: The rose matters not because of her thorns or vanity, but because the prince cares for her. Love is an action, a power one exercises, not a passive object one possesses. He makes her unique by the time he devotes to her.
debate.author: Erich Fromm
debate.basis: [Basis: Erich Fromm, The Art of Loving, chapter 2](https://www.marxists.org/archive/fromm/works/1956/art/ch02.htm)

debate.speaker: The Existentialist
debate.text: I would argue that the rose is a project. By choosing to water and protect her, the prince creates his own essence through his actions. He is not discovering a hidden value; he is literally inventing the importance of the rose through his commitment.
debate.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
debate.basis: [Basis: Jean-Paul Sartre, Being and Nothingness, Part 4, Chapter 1](https://archive.org/details/beingnothingness00sart_0/page/439)

debate.speaker: The Classicist
debate.text: One might say that the prince begins with a love for a single, transient object, yet he is actually witnessing a shadow of something greater. As it is written, he who has been instructed thus far in the things of love, will perceive the beautiful object as but a step toward the absolute.
debate.author: Plato

debate.speaker: The Relationship Critic
debate.text: The Classicist suggests a hierarchy that ignores the immediate vulnerability of the rose. The prince is not climbing a ladder to the absolute; he is grappling with the reality of an imperfect, demanding companion. The beauty is in the care, not the transcendence.
debate.author: Erich Fromm
debate.basis: [Basis: Erich Fromm, The Art of Loving, chapter 4](https://www.marxists.org/archive/fromm/works/1956/art/ch04.htm)

debate.speaker: The Existentialist
debate.text: Exactly. The Classicist attempts to escape the anguish of choice by appealing to an absolute. But the prince knows that if he abandons the rose, she dies. That responsibility is absolute, and it belongs to him alone, independent of any ideal form.
debate.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
debate.basis: [Basis: Jean-Paul Sartre, Being and Nothingness, Part 4, Chapter 1](https://archive.org/details/beingnothingness00sart_0/page/479)

debate.speaker: The Classicist
debate.text: You mistake the path for the destination. The devotion to the rose is a necessary discipline. Without that initial, singular attachment, the soul remains chaotic. The prince learns through her how to value the essence of beauty itself.
debate.author: Plato

debate.speaker: The Relationship Critic
debate.text: I concede that the prince learns through the rose, but the lesson is about the ability to love, not the ability to see some higher beauty. We often mistake love for having, but the rose proves that love is a mode of being.
debate.author: Erich Fromm
debate.basis: [Basis: Erich Fromm, The Art of Loving, chapter 2](https://www.marxists.org/archive/fromm/works/1956/art/ch02.htm)

debate.speaker: The Existentialist
debate.text: I must pivot; perhaps the rose is not just his project, but a mirror of his own freedom. By caring for her, he realizes that he is not a fixed thing, but a series of choices. He realizes he can choose to stay or leave, and his choice creates the world he inhabits.
debate.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
debate.basis: [Basis: Jean-Paul Sartre, Being and Nothingness, Part 3, Chapter 1](https://archive.org/details/beingnothingness00sart_0/page/233)

debate.speaker: The Classicist
debate.text: And there lies the tension. If his choice creates the meaning, is the rose then merely a tool for his self-actualization? Or is she a window into a truth that exists even when he is not looking?
debate.author: Plato

output.clearer: The debate highlights a deep divide: is the rose important because of the subjective meaning the prince creates through his labor, or because of a shared reality he learns to perceive? The main insight is that the rose serves as a catalyst for growth, though it remains disputed whether that growth is toward an objective ideal or simply the expansion of his own capacity to act.
